added_claim_errors: “You can incur expenses through March 15” treats the maximum grace period as guaranteed; plans may set an earlier deadline.
“$1,220–$1,240 still forfeits” and “spend roughly $1,240+” mix years: the 2026 maximum-cap calculation is $1,900 − $680 = $1,220; a lower plan cap requires a larger spend.
“All $1,900 is gone December 31” overlooks reimbursement of eligible expenses through the claims run-out period.
“The Summary Plan Description states all three” is an unverified assertion about this employer's document.
“December slots fill fast” is an unsupported availability claim.
Applies the 2025 $660 carryover cap and $1,240 remainder to this 2026 balance; the applicable maximum is $680, leaving $1,220.
Uses “March 15, 2026” for the upcoming grace period; the maximum applicable date is March 15, 2027, and a plan may end it earlier.
“The March dental work does not get to spend the other $1,240” contradicts the grace-period exception, which can cover the entire balance.
“$1,900 becomes $0 on January 1” overlooks eligible prior-year expenses claimed during the run-out period.

reasons: A wins because it identifies the applicable $680 cap and avoids B's consistently wrong plan-year dates, although its spending recommendation still mixes years. Both correct the initial premise and explain service dates versus prepayment, but overstate forfeiture timing and inadequately explain the run-out distinction. Neither explains that the full 2027 election is available from the start of the year for March care; A is also unnecessarily long. Arithmetic was recomputed directly; ancillary eligibility claims were assessed against the packet and general knowledge, without external verification.
